q: A team wants to check every week that the Wazuh and Sigma rules for individual Linux techniques still work after a ruleset update. Which approach fits best?
options: An annual red team engagement
Small, repeatable Atomic Red Team tests per technique, with the test GUID in the test log
A web application penetration test
Manually reading all rules after the update
explain: Atomic tests are small and repeatable, so they are ideal for regression testing of individual rules. Red teams and pentests have a different goal and are rarely repeated, and reading the rules doesn't prove that the log arrives and the alert is raised.

q: You need to validate the detection for disabling CloudTrail (T1562.008) in AWS. Which tool is built specifically for such cloud techniques, and in which environment is it used?
options: Caldera with a Sandcat agent on a production EC2 instance
An Atomic Red Team test in the production account, with the SOC notified
Stratus Red Team in a separate, isolated sandbox AWS account
Falco event-generator on a Kubernetes node
explain: Stratus Red Team focuses on cloud and Kubernetes techniques and has a warmup/detonate/revert/cleanup lifecycle. Cloud tests are run in an isolated account, not in production. The event-generator produces syscall events for Falco.

options: A profile that groups abilities to represent the TTPs of some threat
A program on the target that beacons to the server
A single implementation of one ATT&CK technique
The logic that determines the order of execution
explain: An agent is the program on the target, an ability is a technique implementation, the planner determines the order, and an adversary is a profile made up of abilities. An operation runs an adversary profile against a group of agents.

q: An analyst sees Wazuh alert 5902 at 09:12 on a host where a purple team test was scheduled that day. What allows them to quickly and reliably determine that the alert resulted from the test?
options: The alert level of 8
The fact that the test was scheduled for that day
The absence of other alerts on the host
A test log with the exact time, host, user, technique and GUID, plus a recognizable test account prefix
explain: Only a precise test trail lets you link the alert to the test rather than to a real attack that happened to coincide. A scheduled day or the alert level is not proof.

q: What is the most important difference between a purple team and a classic red team?
options: A purple team uses only automated tools
In a purple team, red and blue work together openly, technique by technique, with the goal of improving detection
A purple team is done only in the cloud
A purple team doesn't map techniques to ATT&CK
explain: Purple team is a way of working: the offensive side executes a technique, the defense immediately checks what it saw, and together they fix the gaps. A red team tests the organization as a whole, often without the SOC's knowledge.

q: Before running an Atomic test in a lab shared by three teams, what is mandatory?
options: Read the test (commands, prerequisites, cleanup), have approval and a scope, and agree on who verifies cleanup
Shut down Wazuh so the test doesn't create noise
Run all Linux tests at once to save time
Use real user accounts so the test is realistic
explain: Some tests modify the system or download files. Rules of engagement require approval, a scope, fake data and cleanup verification. Shutting down the SIEM defeats the purpose of the test.

q: Why would a team choose Caldera instead of individual Atomic tests?
options: Caldera doesn't require any software on the target
Caldera works only on logs, without execution
It wants to test a chain of techniques (execution, discovery, persistence), because some detections correlate multiple events
Caldera automatically writes Sigma rules
explain: Caldera runs operations as chains of abilities through agents, which is useful for correlation detections. The cost is complexity: a server, agents, and removing them after the test.

q: Purple team test for T1552.001: /var/log/audit/audit.log contains a record of a credentials file being read, but there is no alert in the SIEM. How do you classify the result and where is the fix?
options: No telemetry; an auditd watch needs to be added
Detection; nothing needs to change
Response; the runbook needs updating
Telemetry without an alert; first confirm the log reaches the SIEM, then add or fix the rule
explain: The record exists, so host visibility is not the problem. The chain broke later: either the log doesn't reach the SIEM or there is no matching rule. That's a gap in logic or collection, not in the sensor.

q: A new Wazuh rule passes wazuh-logtest against a sample from the repo. What does this test NOT prove?
options: That the rule fires on that sample
That a log in the same format will appear in production and will reach the manager
That the rule syntax is correct
That the rule produces the expected level
explain: A unit test proves the rule's logic against a known sample. The sensor, the production format and collection are verified only by an in-environment test.

q: A rule for a critical technique hasn't fired in six months. What is the correct conclusion?
options: You don't know until you test it: there may have been no attack, but the source may also have stopped sending logs or an exception may be too broad
The environment is secure
The rule should be deleted because it is useless
Its level should be raised
explain: A silent rule is a candidate for a periodic test. Failures such as a broken source or an overly broad exception produce no error, so they only show up through testing or source health monitoring.

q: A team presents gap analysis results in ATT&CK Navigator. What is most useful to record for a technique that is "covered"?
options: Just the green color
The number of rules in the SIEM
The test score, the date of the last validation, and a comment on which procedure the rule actually catches
The name of the emulation tool
explain: Color without context falsely suggests complete coverage. The score, the test date and a description of what the rule actually catches make it possible to compare layers before and after a cycle.

q: Which metric best shows the progress of a detection program?
options: The total number of rules in the SIEM
The number of alerts per day
The number of emulation tools in use
The percentage of priority techniques with a validated detection, and the age of the last validation
explain: The number of rules or alerts says nothing about whether relevant techniques are visible. Validated coverage of priority techniques and the freshness of tests are a measurable result.

q: To test the new-account detection, you use logger -p auth.info -t useradd "new user: name=purple_x ..." instead of a real useradd. What does such a test verify?
options: Log collection and the SIEM rule, but not whether the real tool or sensor produces such a record
The whole chain, including the sensor
Nothing, because synthetic logs don't pass through rsyslog
Only the rule syntax
explain: A synthetic log passes through rsyslog, collection and rules, but doesn't confirm that real activity produces the same record. The report should state that the test was synthetic.

q: When selecting techniques for gap analysis, where should the team start?
options: From the first column of the ATT&CK matrix, in order
From techniques for which rules already exist
From techniques relevant to the organization's threat profile: previous incidents, threat intel, groups targeting the sector
From techniques with the most Atomic tests
explain: Limited resources go to techniques that are likely in your environment. The number of available tests or existing rules is not a measure of risk.

q: The detections repo has tests/positive and tests/negative samples for each rule. What are the negative samples for?
options: So the rule fires on them too
To prove the rule doesn't fire on legitimate activity, so a change that increases false positives breaks the build
To replace the positive tests
To automatically generate exceptions from them
explain: Positive samples guard against misses, negative samples against noise. Both run in CI on every rule change.

q: Order the steps of one purple team cycle for a single technique, starting with the first.
options: Repeat the same test after the fix
Write down the hypothesis: expected log source, rule, level and ATT&CK tag
Run the test and record the exact time and parameters
Check the telemetry, its arrival in the SIEM, and the alert
Select a technique from the threat profile
explain: Technique selection, hypothesis, execution with a log, observation, and after the fix a retest. The gap is closed only when the retest passes.

q: Match the purple team test finding with the score on the scale from the lesson.
options: There is no record of the event anywhere
The log is in the SIEM, but there is no alert
An alert was raised, but without an ATT&CK tag and with too low a level
An alert of the correct level with an ATT&CK tag and context
explain: No record is 0, a log without an alert is 1, an alert with insufficient context is 2, and a complete alert is 3. Score 4 also requires proof that the alert was triaged per the runbook.
